steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the political context of the European vaccine debate on Twitter. It should give background on vaccine hesitancy and how it connects to social media and politics, point out the research gap, and present our approach, research questions and dataset.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: vaccine hesitancy and COVID-19
- Drivers of hesitancy; echo-chambers online
- Politics and vaccine hesitancy
- Research gap
- Our approach and research questions
- Dataset and political mapping

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - vaccination: reduced mortality, eradicated smallpox; skepticism about safety/efficacy persisted through history
  - COVID-19 vaccines: rapid development, global distribution -> renewed apprehension
  - Eurobarometer, February 2022: most EU citizens support vaccination; worry about unknown long-term side effects 47%–70% by country
  - fully against vaccination: Bulgaria 29%, Slovakia 24%, Slovenia 21%
  - WHO, 2019 (pre-COVID): vaccine hesitancy among top 10 threats to global health
- Drivers of hesitancy; echo-chambers online
  - complex mix of psychological and sociological factors
  - linked to alternative health practices, science denial, conspiratorial thinking
  - must be contextualized: personal experiences/beliefs; societal, public health, communication environments
  - web channels, social networks, recommendation systems -> possible echo-chambers, national and global
  - tightly-knit homogeneous communities = fertile ground for fringe anti-mainstream narratives
  - narratives exclude traditional/authoritative sources; rely on low-quality info and misinformation; undermine trust in public health authorities
- Politics and vaccine hesitancy
  - governments rush to confront COVID-19; political actors join the discussion
  - social media adoption coincides with use by populist/anti-establishment politicians
  - context collapse, bite-size units of communication -> skepticism of authority
  - France, Italy: right-wing party backers had higher unvaccinated rate
  - Poland, ~August 2021: vaccination highest in areas supporting politician opposing ruling conservative Law and Justice (PiS); PiS accused of “flirting” with “anti-vaxxers”
  - U.S., May 2022: Republicans + leaning independents 60% vs Democrats + leaners 85% fully vaccinated
  - across Europe: vaccine hesitancy and political populism positively associated
- Research gap
  - social media use <-> vaccine hesitancy documented
  - little attention to politicized vaccine communication on social media
  - Twitter studies: Japan — criticism of government's vaccine rollout and of holding the 2020 Olympic Games in Tokyo
  - politicians act on public health and medicine, talk to constituents about personal health -> urgent to understand interplay with audience
- Our approach and research questions
  - Twitter; political actors, political interest, consumption of vaccine-hesitant content
  - period immediately before and during onset of COVID-19 epidemic
  - custom network analysis pipeline -> users likely to retweet vaccine-hesitant content; 17 European countries; multilingual, longitudinal dataset
  - extends prior work assuming two-sided controversy; handles multiple “pockets” of opinion; generalizable to multi-sided discourse
  - RQ: are endorsers of vaccine-hesitant content interested in specific parties?
  - RQ: is politicization (interest in politics, focus on few parties) related to endorsement?
  - RQ: are political actors more influential than non-political users?
- Dataset and political mapping
  - multilingual: national discussions in native languages; 16 of 17 countries without English as official language
  - contrast: earlier studies with English-only queries for “worldwide” sentiment
  - mapping Twitter accounts <-> political figures; enriched with ParlGov (parties, elections, cabinets, governments in parliamentary democracies worldwide)
  - first quantitative investigation of political interest on social media vs vaccine hesitancy on a European scale

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Vaccination has been very successful in reducing mortality and in eradicating diseases like smallpox, but skepticism about whether vaccines are safe and effective has been around throughout history anyway. The COVID-19 vaccines were developed fast and distributed globally, and this spurred new apprehension. A Eurobarometer survey in February 2022 found that most EU citizens supported vaccination, but the concerns about unknown long-term side effects of COVID-19 vaccines ranged from 47% to 70% in different countries, and the people who were against vaccination altogether reached 29% in Bulgaria, then 24% in Slovakia and 21% in Slovenia. Even before COVID-19, the World Health Organization indicated vaccine hesitancy as one of the top 10 threats to global health in 2019.

Vaccine hesitancy was found to correlate with a complex combination of psychological and sociological factors. Recent literature links these attitudes with alternative health practices, science denial, and conspiratorial thinking. But this has to be put in the context of personal experiences and beliefs, and of the broader societal, public health and communication environments. There is a concerning trend around web-based communication channels, including social networks and the ones that integrate recommendation systems, which is that echo-chambers can possibly form there, both at national and at global scales. The communities in these echo-chambers are tightly-knit and homogeneous, so they are fertile ground for fringe narratives that oppose the mainstream. These narratives often exclude traditional and authoritative sources and they are supported by low-quality information and misinformation instead, and this undermines the trust in the public health authorities.

When governments around the world rushed to confront the COVID-19 pandemic, many political actors joined the discussion. At the same time, the increasing adoption of social media has coincided with populist and anti-establishment politicians using it, and they took advantage of the context collapse around bite-size units of communication to promote skepticism of authority. Vaccine hesitancy has been linked to political beliefs worldwide, including in France and Italy, where people who backed right-wing parties had a higher unvaccinated rate. In Poland, around August 2021, vaccination rates were highest in the areas that supported the politician opposing the ruling conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, a party which has been accused of “flirting” with “anti-vaxxers”. In the U.S., by May 2022 Republicans and Republican-leaning independents (60%) were less likely to be fully vaccinated than Democrats and Democratic leaners (85%). Overall, studies find that vaccine hesitancy and political populism are positively associated across Europe.

- Research gap
  - social media use <-> vaccine hesitancy documented
  - little attention to politicized vaccine communication on social media
  - Twitter studies: Japan — criticism of government's vaccine rollout and of holding the 2020 Olympic Games in Tokyo
  - politicians act on public health and medicine, talk to constituents about personal health -> urgent to understand interplay with audience
- Our approach and research questions
  - Twitter; political actors, political interest, consumption of vaccine-hesitant content
  - period immediately before and during onset of COVID-19 epidemic
  - custom network analysis pipeline -> users likely to retweet vaccine-hesitant content; 17 European countries; multilingual, longitudinal dataset
  - extends prior work assuming two-sided controversy; handles multiple “pockets” of opinion; generalizable to multi-sided discourse
  - RQ: are endorsers of vaccine-hesitant content interested in specific parties?
  - RQ: is politicization (interest in politics, focus on few parties) related to endorsement?
  - RQ: are political actors more influential than non-political users?
- Dataset and political mapping
  - multilingual: national discussions in native languages; 16 of 17 countries without English as official language
  - contrast: earlier studies with English-only queries for “worldwide” sentiment
  - mapping Twitter accounts <-> political figures; enriched with ParlGov (parties, elections, cabinets, governments in parliamentary democracies worldwide)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Vaccination has been very successful in reducing mortality and in eradicating diseases like smallpox, but skepticism about whether vaccines are safe and effective has been around throughout history anyway. The COVID-19 vaccines were developed fast and distributed globally, and this spurred new apprehension. A Eurobarometer survey in February 2022 found that most EU citizens supported vaccination, but the concerns about unknown long-term side effects of COVID-19 vaccines ranged from 47% to 70% in different countries, and the people who were against vaccination altogether reached 29% in Bulgaria, then 24% in Slovakia and 21% in Slovenia. Even before COVID-19, the World Health Organization indicated vaccine hesitancy as one of the top 10 threats to global health in 2019.

Vaccine hesitancy was found to correlate with a complex combination of psychological and sociological factors. Recent literature links these attitudes with alternative health practices, science denial, and conspiratorial thinking. But this has to be put in the context of personal experiences and beliefs, and of the broader societal, public health and communication environments. There is a concerning trend around web-based communication channels, including social networks and the ones that integrate recommendation systems, which is that echo-chambers can possibly form there, both at national and at global scales. The communities in these echo-chambers are tightly-knit and homogeneous, so they are fertile ground for fringe narratives that oppose the mainstream. These narratives often exclude traditional and authoritative sources and they are supported by low-quality information and misinformation instead, and this undermines the trust in the public health authorities.

When governments around the world rushed to confront the COVID-19 pandemic, many political actors joined the discussion. At the same time, the increasing adoption of social media has coincided with populist and anti-establishment politicians using it, and they took advantage of the context collapse around bite-size units of communication to promote skepticism of authority. Vaccine hesitancy has been linked to political beliefs worldwide, including in France and Italy, where people who backed right-wing parties had a higher unvaccinated rate. In Poland, around August 2021, vaccination rates were highest in the areas that supported the politician opposing the ruling conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, a party which has been accused of “flirting” with “anti-vaxxers”. In the U.S., by May 2022 Republicans and Republican-leaning independents (60%) were less likely to be fully vaccinated than Democrats and Democratic leaners (85%). Overall, studies find that vaccine hesitancy and political populism are positively associated across Europe.

The connection between social media use and vaccine hesitancy has been documented, but little attention has been paid to the connection between politicized communication about vaccination on social media and vaccine hesitancy. Some studies on Twitter have found that politics is part of the conversation, for example COVID-19 vaccine discussions in Japan included criticism of how the government handled the vaccine rollout and of holding the 2020 Olympic Games in Tokyo. Politicians take actions that impact public health and the practice of medicine, including communicating to their constituents on personal health matters, so it is urgent to understand the interplay between these political actors and their audience when it comes to vaccination.

To address this gap, we use Twitter, which is one of the most popular social media platforms, to gauge the relationship between political actors, political interest, and the consumption of vaccine-hesitant content in the period immediately before and during the onset of the COVID-19 epidemic. We propose a custom network analysis pipeline to identify the users that are likely to retweet vaccine-hesitant content in 17 European countries, using a multilingual, longitudinal dataset. Our approach extends previous research which assumes a two-sided controversy, since it also handles multiple “pockets” of opinion stances, so it can be generalized to multi-sided discourse around the world.

With these tools we answer the following research questions:

Are the users more likely to endorse vaccine-hesitant content interested in specific political parties?

Is the politicization of a user (meaning how much they are interested in politics and how much they focus on few parties) related to their endorsement of vaccine-hesitant content?

Are political actors more influential in the vaccination debate than non-political users?

Our dataset is multilingual, and this is crucial because it allows us to examine the national discussions in their native languages: out of the 17 countries we consider, 16 do not have English as an official language (previous studies used English-only queries to analyze “worldwide” vaccine sentiment). We also do an extensive mapping between the Twitter accounts in these countries and their political figures, and we enrich this mapping using ParlGov, which is a political science resource that gives detailed information about political parties, elections, cabinets, and governments in parliamentary democracies worldwide. Combining these resources allowed us to do the first quantitative investigation of the relationship between political interest on social media and vaccine hesitancy on a European scale, as detailed below.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Despite the success of vaccination in reducing mortality and eradicating diseases like smallpox [1], skepticism about vaccine safety and efficacy has persisted throughout history. The rapid development and global distribution of the COVID-19 vaccines spurred new apprehension. In February 2022, a Eurobarometer survey found that while most EU citizens supported vaccination, concerns about unknown long-term side effects of COVID-19 vaccines ranged from 47% to 70% across countries, with those altogether against vaccination reaching 29% in Bulgaria, followed by 24% in Slovakia and 21% in Slovenia [2]. Even before COVID-19, the World Health Organization indicated vaccine hesitancy as one of the top 10 threats to global health in 2019 [3].

Vaccine hesitancy was found to correlate with a complex combination of psychological and sociological factors. Recent literature has linked such attitudes with alternative health practices [4], science denial [5], and conspiratorial thinking [6]. However, this must be put in the context of personal experiences and beliefs, and of the broader societal, public health and communication environments [7]. A concerning trend around web-based communication channels, including social networks and those integrating recommendation systems, is the possible formation of echo-chambers, both at national [8,9] and global scales [10], since the tightly-knit, homogeneous communities in such echo-chambers provide fertile ground for fringe narratives opposing the mainstream [11]. These narratives often exclude traditional and authoritative sources [12] and are instead supported by low-quality information and misinformation [13], which undermines trust in the public health authorities.

As governments around the world rushed to confront the COVID-19 pandemic, various political actors joined the discussion. At the same time, the increasing adoption of social media has coincided with its use by populist and anti-establishment politicians [14], who took advantage of the context collapse around bite-size units of communication to promote skepticism of authority [15]. Worldwide, vaccine hesitancy has been linked to political beliefs, including in France and Italy [16,17], where those backing right-wing parties had a higher unvaccinated rate. In Poland, around August 2021 vaccination rates were highest in the areas supporting the politician opposing the ruling conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – a party accused of “flirting” with “anti-vaxxers” [18]. In the U.S., by May 2022 Republicans and Republican-leaning independents (60%) were less likely to be fully vaccinated than Democrats and Democratic leaners (85%) [19]. Overall, studies find vaccine hesitancy and political populism to be positively associated across Europe [20,21].

Although the connection between social media use and vaccine hesitancy has been documented [13,22], little attention has been paid to the connection between politicized communication around vaccination on social media and vaccine hesitancy. For instance, some studies on Twitter have found politics to be part of the conversation: COVID-19 vaccine-related discussions in Japan included criticism of the government’s handling of the vaccine rollout and of the holding of the 2020 Olympic Games in Tokyo [23]. As politicians take actions that impact public health and the practice of medicine, including communicating to their constituents on matters of personal health [24], it is urgent to understand the interplay between such political actors and their audience in the context of vaccination.

To address this research gap, we turn to Twitter, one of the most popular social media platforms, to gauge the relationship between political actors, political interest, and the consumption of vaccine-hesitant content in the period immediately before and during the onset of the COVID-19 epidemic. We propose a custom network analysis pipeline to identify users likely to retweet vaccine-hesitant content in 17 European countries using a multilingual, longitudinal dataset. Our approach extends previous research [25] that assumes a two-sided controversy by also handling multiple “pockets” of opinion stances, which makes it generalizable to multi-sided discourse around the world.

Using these tools, we answer the following research questions:

Are those more likely to endorse vaccine-hesitant content interested in specific political parties?

Is a user’s politicization (i.e. how interested they are in politics and how much they focus on few parties) related to their endorsement of vaccine-hesitant content?

Are political actors more influential in the vaccination debate than non-political users?

Crucially, our multilingual dataset lets us examine the national discussions in their native languages, as 16 of the 17 countries considered do not have English as an official language (unlike previous studies that use English-only queries to analyze “worldwide” vaccine sentiment [26,27]). Further, we perform an extensive mapping between the Twitter accounts in these countries and their respective political figures, which we then enrich using ParlGov [28], a political science resource providing detailed information about political parties, elections, cabinets, and governments in parliamentary democracies worldwide. Combining these resources has allowed us to complete the first quantitative investigation of the relationship between political interest on social media and vaccine hesitancy on a European scale, as detailed below.

References:
[1] Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Impact of vaccines universally recommended for children–united states, 1990-1998. MMWR. Morbidity and mortality weekly report 48 , 243–248 (1999).
[2] Flash Eurobarometer 505. Attitudes on vaccination against covid-19 - february 2022. https://www.quotidianosanita.it/allegati/allegato1650373320.pdf (2022).
[3] World Health Organization. Ten threats to global health 2019. https://www.who.int/news-room/spotlight/ten-threats-to-global-health-in-2019 (2019).
